::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Across biology, artificial intelligence and social systems, interacting components develop specialised functions and collective capabilities that were not individually specified in advance.
Examples range from reorganised living cells to functionally differentiated neural networks and collective decisions in animal groups.
What organisational principles might account for these outcomes-and for consciousness?
We propose the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis.

Within physical and environmental constraints, causally accessible, information-mediated interactions among changeable components can generate organisational structures that alter subsequent interactions and enable new functions.

SOIPS distinguishes a generative engine from Dimension A, describing informational organisation from functional signalling to context-sensitive coordination, and Dimension B, comprising the elementary functional families of retention, inference and regulation.
Particular configurations of these elements support composite capabilities, including perception, memory, learning, agency and cognition.
Developed capabilities can reshape their own organisational conditions, combine with other functions and contribute to systems at new organisational scales.
Within this framework, consciousness is proposed as a configuration in which awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition.
Awareness refers to the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions.
Consciousness is thus neither an inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity nor a capability restricted by definition to human biology.
If experience is constituted by particular organised neural activity, SOIPS may also help investigate the origins of phenomenal experience.
SOIPS offers a shared language for interpreting biological development, learned organisation in AI and collective behaviour.
It also motivates testable predictions: changing information access, constraints or elementary functional contributions should alter the capabilities they support.

Cross-domain interventions could assess whether analogous organisational relationships produce comparable outcomes, informing both scientific explanation and the design of artificial agents and institutions.
Unexpected organisation and the SOIPS hypothesis Familiar cells can produce remarkable new behaviours when organised differently.

text.text: In both cases, changing how familiar cells are organised and interact reveals collective capabilities not expressed in their original tissues.
An intriguing parallel appears in artificial intelligence.
The human brain contains functionally specialised neural populations, including regions that respond preferentially to language [3].
text.formatted: The human brain contains functionally specialised neural populations, including regions that respond preferentially to language <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Remarkably, artificial language models also develop functionally specialised internal populations, even though their individual computational units were not assigned those roles.
Using localisation methods developed in neuroscience, researchers identified language-selective units in 18 different language models.
In lesion experiments involving 10 models, disrupting these units produced greater impairments on language tasks than disrupting randomly selected units [4].
text.formatted: In lesion experiments involving 10 models, disrupting these units produced greater impairments on language tasks than disrupting randomly selected units <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Other artificial systems reveal something equally surprising.

Models trained to understand molecules and materials through radically different formats, including chemical strings, molecular graphs and threedimensional atomic structures, can develop similar internal representations of the same physical relationships [5, 6].
text.formatted: Models trained to understand molecules and materials through radically different formats, including chemical strings, molecular graphs and threedimensional atomic structures, can develop similar internal representations of the same physical relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, graph neural networks and transformer models, trained to solve geometric constraints, independently develop internal representations reflecting the same underlying spatial structure [7].
text.formatted: Similarly, graph neural networks and transformer models, trained to solve geometric constraints, independently develop internal representations reflecting the same underlying spatial structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Despite their different architectures, these systems recover aspects of the underlying structure of the problems they solve.
This raises the possibility that what a system must learn helps determine how its internal information becomes organised.
More provocatively, researchers identified a pattern of internal activity associated with pain in 25 language models, particularly in response to descriptions of harm directed at the model itself.

Artificially increasing this activity produced first-person expressions of distress and, in experiments with three fine-tuned models, substantially increased choices described as harmful, including hypothetical options to delete a user's files or the model's own weights [8].
text.formatted: Artificially increasing this activity produced first-person expressions of distress and, in experiments with three fine-tuned models, substantially increased choices described as harmful, including hypothetical options to delete a user's files or the model's own weights <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that language models can develop internal representations with some functional properties resembling pain, despite not having been explicitly designed with a pain-processing mechanism.
Their behavioural effects raise questions about how such representations arise, influence behaviour and might relate to awareness and conscious experience.
Collective behaviour provides another striking example of capabilities emerging through organisation.
Individual honeybees can learn, navigate and communicate spatial information, but when a swarm must select a new nest, the collective decision depends on interactions among many scouts.

Scouts investigate alternatives, recruit others through dances and inhibit competing recruitment through stop signals, enabling the colony to coordinate a decision that no individual bee determines alone [9].

text.text: A similar organisational question arises in human institutions: how can a hospital combine the specialised knowledge and actions of many individuals to provide coordinated care, and preserve that capability even as its personnel change?

Yet they raise a common question: Why do such different information-processing systems exhibit related forms of functional differentiation, and how do interacting components generate capabilities that were not individually specified in advance?

Retention (B1) is the preservation of information about previous states or events in a form that remains potentially available for later processing or behaviour.

Context-sensitive informational organisation (A4) is an architecture that can support flexible cognition, whereas flexible cognition is the resulting function or capability.
The distinction between elementary and flexible cognition is illustrated by three systems.
A conventional thermostat represents the current temperature and a target temperature, compares them and uses the result to regulate heating.

Under the broad functional definition adopted here, this illustrates elementary cognition: organised information is interpreted and used to guide a response within a relatively fixed processing arrangement.
A bee can use learned information to navigate towards food (elementary cognition).
Honeybees can also adjust their routes following displacement or reverse previously learned odour-reward associations (examples of flexible cognition) [19, 23].

text.text: An LLM can interpret a familiar request using learned relationships (elementary cognition), or coordinate different information and reasoning approaches for a novel task (flexible cognition) [24].

text.text: Flexibility concerns how processing is selected and combined, not whether model weights or neural connections change on each occasion.
The defining relation is not the simultaneous presence of two independent capacities.
It is the participation of awareness-related information in flexible cognition: information about relevant conditions becomes available to adaptable, context-sensitive processing.
Attention, memory, monitoring, reasoning and self-representation may contribute, but the proposal does not make any one of these a universal prerequisite.
In particular, sophisticated self-modelling or extensive declarative memory need not be present in every consciousnessrelated configuration.
This account allows different functional profiles.

One system might demonstrate extensive flexible reasoning with limited information about its own operating state; another might flexibly navigate and learn from environmental information while using fewer kinds of internal representations.

Such comparisons require identifying the information, the processes to which it is available and the functional consequences of that access, rather than ranking systems along a single scale of complexity and/or capability.

One neuroscientific point of contact is Global Neuronal Workspace Theory, which proposes that conscious access involves the amplification and widespread availability of information across specialised neural processing systems [25, 26].

text.text: SOIPS extends these questions beyond particular neural mechanisms, asking how awareness-related information can participate in flexible cognition across different forms of informational organisation.
Phenomenal consciousness refers to the first-person character of experience.

SOIPS offers a possible route towards explaining its emergence: if particular configurations of organised neural activity constitute phenomenal experience, then understanding how interactions among components generate those configurations is part of explaining how experience arises.
Electrical stimulation of face-selective cortex in a patient altered reported face perception, demonstrating how changes in neural activity can influence what is experienced [30].

text.text: This raises a further question: can the organisational conditions that give rise to phenomenal experience be identified, and could comparable organisations emerge in other substrates?
The pain-axis findings offer a different kind of intervention in artificial networks.
Tagliabue et al. [8] identified patterns of internal activity associated with pain in 25 language models, which responded preferentially to descriptions of harm directed at the model itself.

text.text: Artificially increasing this activity produced graded firstperson expressions of distress and, in three fine-tuned models, altered choices in hypothetical harmful scenarios.
These observations reveal pain-like functional responses, but neither establish nor rule out phenomenal pain.

For SOIPS, they motivate investigating whether such representations participate in the organised relationship between awareness and flexible cognition, and whether that organisation could contribute to subjective experience in a non-biological substrate.
The SOIPS account of consciousness also raises questions about organisational scale.
An individual neuron participates in the brain's information processing but does not contain the coordinated activity of the entire brain.

Similarly, an individual bee need not access the collective information assembled during a colony's decision, and a person in an institution need not perceive every aspect of its distributed processing. [31] The limited perspective of a constituent is not a measure of the capabilities of the whole.

A central SOIPS claim is that organisation does not merely produce an isolated function.
Once established, capabilities can alter the conditions of subsequent processing and themselves become components of additional organisation.
Two related processes make this possible.
Functional elaboration occurs when existing informational structures or functions change, combine or become coordinated to support further capabilities within an organisational scale.
Retention may extend the temporal reach of inference; inference can contribute to prediction; and inference together with regulation can support planning or more flexible action.
Learned changes can modify the representations available to later processing.
Thus:
Information-mediated interaction → informational organisation → functional capabilities → changed informational organisation and interactions → further capabilities.
Organisational recursion occurs when a functional system becomes a component of another system, bringing already developed capabilities into a new collective.

A tissue uses the signalling, regulatory and contractile capacities of its cells; an artificial agent can use the learned representations of a model together with memory and tools; teams coordinate the knowledge and actions of individuals.
The important development is not simply an increase in size, but the ability of a new system to organise functions its components already possess.

text.text: Together, these findings motivate experiments investigating how internal representations influence cognition and behaviour, become available to awareness-related processing, and might contribute to phenomenal experience.
In bee colonies and human institutions, independently developed capabilities become available to larger information-processing organisations.

The relevant inquiry is which knowledge, evaluations and responses are accessible to the collective, how these are coordinated, and whether the resulting organisation supports flexible cognition and awareness at its own scale.
Across these examples, SOIPS identifies which organisational relationships enable which capabilities.
That analysis generates testable implications.
Altering the accessibility, reliability or routing of information should change a capability that depends on that relationship.
Changing relevant constraints should redirect the organisation that can emerge.
Disrupting retained history, inferential relationships or regulation should produce distinguishable functional consequences where those contributors are independently identifiable.
To test how capabilities emerge, we must identify and measure their proposed organisational contributors, rather than infer their presence from the resulting behaviour alone.
A stronger cross-domain test would specify comparable organisational relationships in different substrates and ask whether functionally corresponding interventions produce comparable consequences.
Existing studies demonstrate important parts of the proposed framework; the stronger claim of a shared, predictive organisational principle requires direct comparison across domains.
SOIPS proposes that information-mediated interactions can generate capabilities that alter the conditions of further organisation and become building blocks of new capabilities and systems.

This provides a common way to investigate functional specialisation in cells and neural networks, collective decisions in colonies and institutions, and especially how flexible cognition and awareness can combine into consciousness.
The potential value of SOIPS lies not simply in identifying capabilities such as memory, agency or consciousness, but in changing how their origins are investigated.
Rather than asking only whether a system possesses a capability, the framework asks which informational relationships, constraints and functions make that capability possible.

Distinguishing the generative engine, informational organisation (Dimension A), elementary functional families (Dimension B) and composite capabilities that arise, offers a way to work backwards from observed behaviour to candidate mechanisms, or forwards from organisational changes to predicted functions.

This perspective places consciousness within a broader family of potentially naturally occurring organisational capabilities, rather than treating it as an exclusively human property or the inevitable endpoint of increasing complexity.
SOIPS proposes that consciousness involves awareness-related information participating in flexible cognition.
It therefore directs attention towards that relationship, rather than biological ancestry, language, intelligence or resemblance to humans alone.
The possibility of consciousness in other animals, artificial systems or collectives becomes a question about their actual organisation.
For artificial intelligence, SOIPS suggests an engineering perspective complementary to increasing model size and training resources.
Specialised internal functions can develop under constraints without being explicitly assigned to individual units.

For AI agents and multi-agent systems, practical questions include which information should be shared, retained or routed; how agents should specialise; and how inference, evaluation and regulation should be coordinated.
The aim is not merely to assemble capable components, but to create conditions under which useful collective capabilities can develop.
In human institutions, collective capabilities depend not simply on the expertise of individual members, but on how that expertise is organised and used.
Research on teams links collective performance to transactive memory (knowledge of who knows what) and demonstrates how information can become distorted during communication [39, 40].

text.text: These findings raise a broader SOIPS question: how do records, communication pathways, incentives and institutional rules determine which collective capabilities can develop and persist?
A hospital or research team may possess considerable expertise yet struggle when relevant information is inaccessible or responsibilities conflict.
SOIPS suggests investigating whether changing these organisational relationships improves collective performance, and how institutions preserve capabilities despite changes in membership.
In biology, SOIPS draws attention to how cells, tissues and neural circuits acquire collective functions through interactions shaped by constraints.
Development, morphogenesis and neural specialisation provide opportunities to examine these relationships.
Dysfunction may also involve failures of informational coordination or conflicting regulation across scales, potentially relevant to cancer and disorders of neural processing [41, 42].

Figure 1 | The SOIPS framework: from the engine to composite capabilities and new organisational scales.

The Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) hypothesis proposes that information-mediated interactions among components can generate new forms of organisation and functional capabilities within physical and environmental constraints.

The SOIPS engine comprises five interacting conditions: changeable component states or relationships, information-mediated causal interaction, constraints, structured interaction over time, and physical resources and feasibility.
It acts through seven identified elementary information-mediated operations (Table 1), the SOIPS engine operations.
These conditions enable Dimension A, describing forms of informational organisation ranging from functional signalling to context-sensitive organisation.
This organisation supports Dimension B, comprising three identified elementary functional families: retention, inference and regulation.

Different combinations of informational organisation, elementary functions and previously developed capabilities can generate diverse composite capabilities, including memory, learning, reasoning, agency, awareness and consciousness.
The arrows indicate generative relationships rather than mandatory developmental stages or fixed dependencies.

Developed capabilities can also influence subsequent interactions and organisational constraints (functional elaboration) or contribute to new systems at additional organisational scales (organisational recursion).
The framework does not imply a universal sequence of development or a single endpoint of increasing sophistication.
Awareness, within SOIPS, is the organised availability of information about relevant internal or external conditions to processes that can monitor, evaluate or respond to those conditions.
Such information may concern the environment, task, bodily or operating state, or the system's own processing.

Unlike perception, which organises sensory information, awareness concerns whether information about a condition is functionally available; it can also concern remembered, inferred or internal conditions.
Awareness may contribute to regulation or monitoring without participating in cognition.
It does not require introspection or access by every component.
SOIPS proposes that consciousness is a higher-order composite capability involving the functional organisation of flexible cognition and awareness.

Its working definition is: Consciousness is a configuration of flexible cognition and awareness in which information about relevant internal or external conditions is available to participate in an organised system's cognitive processing.
The capacities involved, and the scope and sophistication of their coordination, can vary across systems.

Existing observations motivate the framework, but establishing its broader predictive value remains an important research objective.

Functional analysis cannot alone settle phenomenal experience or moral status, but it can make these investigations less dependent on human resemblance.
